issues.legal_issue: A will is proved when its execution and the testator’s capacity are established and any suspicious circumstances are satisfactorily explained.
material_facts: The beneficiaries relied on a will to defeat the deceased’s relatives’ claim to his separate properties.
The scribe testified that the testator instructed him, read the will before signing it, and signed it in the presence of the attesting witnesses, who attested in his presence.

The testator was elderly and had suffered a fracture, but the evidence showed that he was mentally alert; there was no evidence that he had become senile, and he had recently dealt with another property.

The testator’s relationship with his real sister was not cordial, he lived with and was cared for by his stepsister and the beneficiaries, and the claimants were absent during his hospitalization and treatment.

The scribe and witnesses supported execution of the will, and the evidence indicated that the beneficiary who brought them did so at the testator’s request. The testator had declined advice to register the will because he expected to live longer.
issues.conclusion: The beneficiaries proved the execution, attestation, capacity, and genuineness of the will; the unexplained-suspicion challenge did not justify rejecting it.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder bears the burden of proving a will. Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the will must be proved through the legally required execution and attestation, together with proof of the testator’s capacity. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must explain them to the Court’s satisfaction. Suspicion must be assessed in the circumstances of the particular case and cannot replace proof. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, Ryali Kameswara Rao v. Bendapudi Suryaprakasarao, and Sm. Chinmoyee Saha v. Debendra Lal Saha.

rule.if: will_validity_dispute and testator_signed_will and execution_and_attestation_proved and testator_had_capacity and suspicious_circumstances_explained

predicates.will_validity_dispute: A party relied on a will in a dispute over who was entitled to the deceased’s property.
predicates.testator_signed_will: The evidence showed that the testator signed the will.
predicates.execution_and_attestation_proved: The evidence showed that the will was prepared on the testator’s instructions and signed and attested in the legally required presence of the testator and witnesses.
predicates.testator_had_capacity: The evidence showed that the testator understood the will and was mentally capable when it was made.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_explained: The evidence explained circumstances raised against the will, including the testator’s reasons for excluding relatives and the beneficiary’s role in bringing the scribe and witnesses.

issues.definition: When a will is disputed, proof of the testator’s signature, proper execution and attestation, capacity, and satisfactory explanation of suspicious circumstances results in the will being treated as proved.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that a will was forged or procured through undue influence cannot rest on suspicion where the challenger did not plead and prove that allegation.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration and possession, while the beneficiaries relied on the will.
The High Court found that the claimants had not pleaded forgery or undue influence, although particulars of the will had been supplied to them.
The lower appellate court inferred forgery from circumstances including the beneficiaries’ involvement in bringing witnesses, the use of different ink, and the failure to register the will earlier.

The evidence showed that the beneficiary brought the scribe at the testator’s request; the testator read the will before signing it; and no suggestion was put to a witness that the signature was not the testator’s.

The Supreme Court found that the challenger bore the burden of proving forgery, undue influence, or collusion, and that the lower appellate court had no proper basis to find forgery in the absence of the required plea and proof.
issues.conclusion: The lower appellate court erred in holding that the will was forged; the challenge based on that finding failed.
issues.legal_principle: A person alleging forgery, fraud, coercion, undue influence, or collusion must plead and prove the allegation; motive or opportunity, or suspicion alone, is insufficient. Once the propounder establishes prima facie proof of execution and capacity, the contestant may produce material to meet that case, after which the propounder may have to satisfy the Court that the testator understood and freely made the will. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, Ryali Kameswara Rao v. Bendapudi Suryaprakasarao, and Sm. Chinmoyee Saha v. Debendra Lal Saha.

predicates.will_challenge_proceeding: A proceeding challenged a will relied on to determine entitlement to property.
predicates.challenger_did_not_plead_forgery_or_undu: The person challenging the will did not plead that it was forged or procured by undue influence.
predicates.challenger_did_not_prove_forgery_or_undu: The person challenging the will did not produce proof establishing forgery or undue influence.
predicates.suspicion_is_the_basis_for_forgery_findi: The finding of forgery or undue influence rested on suspicious circumstances rather than proof of the alleged misconduct.

issues.definition: In a proceeding challenging a will, absent a pleaded and proved allegation of forgery or undue influence, suspicion alone does not support a finding that the will was forged or procured by undue influence.
